drivel

DRIV-uhl -- from Old English dreflian, originally meaning 'to dribble or drool.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Drivel is silly, nonsensical talk or writing.

Fans booed when the once-beloved podcast host's rambling new episode turned out to be forty minutes of pure drivel.

Worked Example

After three energy drinks and no sleep, his term paper had dissolved into pure drivel by the final page.

The exhausted writing no longer makes any real sense -- it's just nonsensical, low-quality rambling, which is exactly what drivel means.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

claptrap: Claptrap is showy, empty talk designed to win applause or votes -- it takes an audience and a speaker trying to impress. Drivel needs no audience and no strategy: it is simply silly, worthless talk or writing. A campaign speech can be claptrap; a rambling diary page is drivel.

hogwash: Hogwash is nonsense you are calling false -- you say it when someone presents an untrue claim as fact. Drivel is emptier: it condemns talk or writing for being silly and worthless, whether or not it claims anything. Hogwash attacks a statement's truth; drivel attacks its value.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

wisdom: deep understanding and good judgment

insight: a clear, deep understanding of something

Where it sits · how little sense it makes — twaddle → drivel → gibberish

twaddle vs. drivel: Twaddle is milder than drivel: twaddle is merely trivial, off-topic chatter about the weather, while drivel is talk so silly and empty it deserves no attention at all.

gibberish vs. drivel: Gibberish is more extreme than drivel: drivel is silly but still readable, while notes that have dissolved into gibberish cannot be understood by anyone at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — drivel- (Old English dreflian)

root — drivel- (Old English dreflian): to dribble, drool (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Drivel began as a literal word for drooling or dribbling saliva -- over centuries, it drifted into a figurative sense for talk that seems just as messy and pointless.

Use the root in a new word: driveling

Use the root in a new word: driveling: The old, literal sense survives in the now-rare word driveling, once used to describe an old man 'driveling' at the mouth.

Word Building

Word Choice

Drivel is a dismissive, often insulting word -- calling something drivel isn't a neutral description, it's a judgment that the writing or talk has no real value at all.
